title: A page a screen reader can walk

terminal.description: The page runs in the Browser panel and reloads every time you save. The shell is here if you want to look around the files.

tasks.title: Mark the parts of the page
tasks.description:
Give the page its landmarks in `index.html`, so a screen reader can jump between them.

The check looks for:

- a `<header>` around the library name and the menu, outside `<main>`
- a `<nav>` that holds the menu links, outside `<main>`
- exactly one `<main>`, and the page title, the events and the sign-up form are inside it
- a `<footer>` around the "Visit us" block, outside `<main>`

Keep the classes and ids the elements already have. They are what the stylesheet hangs on.
nextSteps: Read the page in the Browser panel and name its four big parts out loud.
Find the `div` that starts each part in `index.html`.
Swap each one for the element that says what it is. Change the closing tag too.
Save, check the page still looks the same, and press Check.
hints: Most of the work is renaming tags. The attributes on each `div` can stay as they are.
There are four parts: the strip at the top, the menu inside it, the middle of the page, and the block at the bottom.

The `div` with class `top` is the start of the page and the `div` with class `menu` sits inside it. The `div` with class `content` and the one with id `visit` are the other two. Each element's name is a plain English word for its part.

tasks.title: Turn the big text into headings
tasks.description:
Replace the text that only looks like a heading with real headings in `index.html`.

The check looks for:

- exactly one `<h1>`, and its text is `What's on in December`
- the titles `Events`, `Save a place` and `Visit us` are headings
- the five event titles are headings
- no level is skipped: going down the page, each heading is at most one level deeper than the one before it

The text of each heading stays exactly as it is now.
nextSteps: List every bit of big or bold text on the page and decide its level.
Make the section titles one level below it and the event titles one level below those.
Remove the `font-weight` from the style attributes you no longer need, then press Check.
hints: Think of the page as a table of contents. Which titles belong under which?
A `<b>` only changes how text looks. A heading also tells a screen reader where a new part starts.
There are three levels: the page title, then the three section titles, then the event titles, which live under Events.

tasks.title: List the events with real dates
tasks.description:
Mark up the event cards so a screen reader knows how many there are and a computer can read their dates.

The check looks for:

- each of the five events is an `<article>` (keep the class `event` on it)
- each article sits in its own `<li>`, and all five are in one `<ul>` or `<ol>` (keep the class `event-list` on the list)
- each event's date is inside a `<time>` whose `datetime` attribute is the date as `YYYY-MM-DD`, optionally followed by `T` and the start time as `HH:MM`

The visible date can read however you like. Write the `datetime` from the date on the card.
nextSteps: Turn the `div` with class `event-list` into a list.
Wrap each card in a list item and turn the card itself into an article.
Wrap each date in a `time` element and write its `datetime`.
If the list shows bullets, add a rule for `.event-list` in `styles.css`, then press Check.
hints: The cards are a set of things of the same kind. Which HTML structure says "here are five things"?
A list item holds an article, which holds the image, the heading, the date, the text and the footer of the card.
December 2026 dates look like `2026-12-05`. With a start time: `2026-12-05T10:00`, in 24-hour time.
